From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The Amen break is a drum break that has been widely sampled in popular music. It comes from the 1969 track "Amen, Brother" by the American soul group the Winstons, released as the B-side of the 1969 single "Color Him Father". The drum break lasts seven seconds and was performed by Gregory Coleman.

With the rise of hip-hop in the 1980s, the Amen break was used in hits including "Straight Outta Compton" by N.W.A and "Keep It Going Now" by Rob Base & DJ E-Z Rock. In the 1990s, it became a staple of drum and bass and jungle music. It has been used in thousands of tracks of various genres, making it one of the most sampled recordings in music history.

The Winstons received no royalties for the sample. The bandleader, Richard Lewis Spencer, was not aware of its use until 1996, after the statute of limitations for copyright infringement had passed. He condemned its use as plagiarism, but later said it was flattering. He said it was unlikely that Coleman, who died homeless and destitute in 2006, realized the impact he had made on music. In 2026, "Amen, Brother" was selected by the US Library of Congress for preservation in the National Recording Registry.

The Winstons were a soul band from Washington, D.C., who played throughout the southern United States. They were led by Richard Lewis Spencer.[1] In early 1969, the Winstons recorded the single "Color Him Father" in Atlanta.[2] For the B-side, they recorded an instrumental based on the gospel song "Amen" and a guitar riff Curtis Mayfield had played for Spencer.[2][3] The result was "Amen, Brother",[3] which Spencer said they composed in about 20 minutes.[2] Though "Color Him Father" became a top-10 R&B hit and won a Grammy Award, "Amen, Brother" received little notice.[2] As a mixed-race group, the Winstons struggled to secure bookings and disbanded in 1970.[2]

At about 1 minute and 26 seconds into "Amen, Brother", the other musicians stop playing and the drummer, Gregory Coleman, performs a four-bar drum break that lasts for seven seconds. For two bars, Coleman plays the previous beat. In the third bar, he delays a snare hit. In the fourth bar, he leaves the first beat empty, then plays a syncopated pattern and an early crash cymbal.[3]

The drum break was added to lengthen the track, which had been too short with just the riff. Spencer said he directed the break, but Phil Tolotta, the only other surviving member of the Winstons in 2015, credited it solely to Coleman.[2]

In the 1980s, with the rise of hip-hop, DJs began using turntables to loop drum breaks from records, which MCs would rap over.[3] In 1986, "Amen, Brother" was included on Ultimate Breaks and Beats, a compilation of old funk and soul tracks with clean drum breaks intended for DJs.[3] Salt-N-Pepa's 1986 single "I Desire" was one of the first tracks to sample the Amen break.[4]

In 1988, Mantronix released the influential track "King of the Beats", which edited and processed the Amen break to make it "central to the track rather than simply a rhythmic bedding".[3] The break was used in a number of mainstream tracks that year, including "Straight Outta Compton" by N.W.A and "Keep It Going Now" by Rob Base & DJ E-Z Rock.[4] It was widely sampled in British dance music in the early 1990s, especially in drum and bass and jungle.[5][3] It has been used in multiple genres, including rock music by acts such as Oasis, in commercials, and television themes such as Futurama.[3][6]

The Amen break has been in used in thousands of tracks, making it one of the most widely sampled tracks in history.[3] It became popular as it was easy to manipulate and offered a simple way to create jungle music.[3] The English drummer Tom Skinner cited the appealing "crunch" of the recording quality.[3] Producers have manipulated it by altering its pitch or speed, or re-ordering its components to mimic ghost notes or other effects.[3]

The copyright owner of "Amen, Brother", including the Amen break, was the Winstons bandleader, Richard Lewis Spencer.[3] Neither he nor Coleman received royalties for the break.[3] Spencer was not aware of its use until an executive contacted him asking for the master tape in 1996, when he was working for the Washington Metro.[3][7] The journalist Simon Reynolds likened the situation to "the man who goes to the sperm bank and unknowingly sires hundreds of children".[3] Spencer was unable to take legal action, as the statute of limitations for copyright infringement at the time was three years.[1]

Spencer condemned the sampling as plagiarism and said he "felt ripped off and raped".[2] He said in 2011: "[Coleman's] heart and soul went into that drum break. Now these guys copy and paste it and make millions."[3] However, in 2015, he said: "It's not the worst thing that can happen to you. I'm a black man in America and the fact that someone wants to use something I created – that's flattering."[2]

Coleman died homeless and destitute in 2006. Spencer said it was unlikely he was aware of the impact he had made on music.[2] In 2015, a GoFundMe campaign set up for Spencer by the British DJs Martyn Webster and Steve Theobald raised more than £18,000 ($26,000).[2] Spencer died in 2020.[8] In 2026, "Amen, Brother" was selected by the US Library of Congress for preservation in the National Recording Registry for its "cultural, historical or aesthetic importance in the nation's recorded sound heritage".[9]

blocks.html_en: The copyright owner of "Amen, Brother", including the Amen break, was the Winstons bandleader, Richard Lewis Spencer.[3] Neither he nor Coleman received royalties for the break.[3] Spencer was not aware of its use until an executive contacted him asking for the master tape in 1996, when he was working for the Washington Metro.[3][7] The journalist Simon Reynolds likened the situation to "the man who goes to the sperm bank and unknowingly sires hundreds of children".[3] Spencer was unable to take legal action, as the statute of limitations for copyright infringement at the time was three years.[1]

blocks.html_en: Spencer condemned the sampling as plagiarism and said he "felt ripped off and raped".[2] He said in 2011: "[Coleman's] heart and soul went into that drum break. Now these guys copy and paste it and make millions."[3] However, in 2015, he said: "It's not the worst thing that can happen to you. I'm a black man in America and the fact that someone wants to use something I created – that's flattering."[2]

blocks.html_en: Coleman died homeless and destitute in 2006. Spencer said it was unlikely he was aware of the impact he had made on music.[2] In 2015, a GoFundMe campaign set up for Spencer by the British DJs Martyn Webster and Steve Theobald raised more than £18,000 ($26,000).[2] Spencer died in 2020.[8] In 2026, "Amen, Brother" was selected by the US Library of Congress for preservation in the National Recording Registry for its "cultural, historical or aesthetic importance in the nation's recorded sound heritage".[9]

content_html_zh:
来自免费百科全书维基百科

阿门休息是一种鼓乐休息，在流行音乐中被广泛采用。 它来自美国灵魂乐团温斯顿乐队 1969 年的歌曲“阿门，兄弟”，作为 1969 年单曲“Color Him Father”的 B 面发行。 鼓声持续七秒，由格雷戈里·科尔曼演奏。

随着 20 世纪 80 年代嘻哈音乐的兴起，Amen Break 被用于热门歌曲中，包括 N.W.A 的“Straight Outta Compton”以及 Rob Base 和 DJ E-Z Rock 的“Keep It Going Now”。 在 20 世纪 90 年代，它成为鼓、贝斯和丛林音乐的主要内容。 它已被用于各种流派的数千首曲目中，使其成为音乐史上采样次数最多的录音之一。

温斯顿夫妇没有收到样品的版税。 乐队指挥 Richard Lewis Spencer 直到 1996 年版权侵权诉讼时效过后才知道它的使用。 他谴责其使用为抄袭，但后来表示这是奉承。 他说，科尔曼于 2006 年无家可归、一贫如洗地去世，他不太可能意识到自己对音乐的影响。 2026年，《阿门，兄弟》被美国国会图书馆选入国家档案登记处保存。

温斯顿乐队是一支来自华盛顿特区的灵魂乐队，他们的演出足迹遍及美国南部。 他们由理查德·刘易斯·斯宾塞领导。[1] 1969 年初，温斯顿夫妇在亚特兰大录制了单曲“Color Him Father”。[2]对于 B 面，他们根据福音歌曲“阿门”录制了一首器乐，以及柯蒂斯·梅菲尔德为斯宾塞演奏的吉他即兴演奏。[2][3]结果是“阿门，兄弟”，[3]斯宾塞说他们在大约 20 分钟内创作了这首歌曲。[2]尽管《Color Him Father》成为 R&B 排行榜前十名并获得了格莱美奖，但《Amen, Brother》却没有引起多少关注。[2]作为一个混血团体，温斯顿乐队 (Winstons) 难以获得预订并于 1970 年解散。 [2]

在《阿门，兄弟》进行到大约 1 分 26 秒时，其他音乐家停止演奏，鼓手格雷戈里·科尔曼 (Gregory Coleman) 演奏了持续七秒的四小节鼓乐。 对于两个小节，科尔曼演奏前一个节拍。 在第三小节中，他延迟了军鼓的击打。 在第四小节中，他将第一拍留空，然后演奏切分音模式和早期的碎钹。 [3]

添加鼓点是为了延长音轨，因为只有即兴重复段的音轨太短了。 斯宾塞表示，这次突破是他指挥的，但 2015 年温斯顿家族中唯一幸存的另一位成员菲尔·托洛塔 (Phil Tolotta) 将其完全归功于科尔曼。 [2]

20 世纪 80 年代，随着嘻哈音乐的兴起，DJ 开始使用转盘循环播放唱片中的鼓点，然后由 MC 进行说唱。 [3] 1986 年，“Amen, Brother”被收录在 Ultimate Breaks and Beats 中，这是一张专为 DJ 准备的带有干净鼓点的老式放克和灵魂曲目合辑。[3] Salt-N-Pepa 1986 年的单曲“I Desire”是第一批采样 Amen Break 的曲目之一。[4]

1988年，Mantronix发行了颇具影响力的曲目“King of the Beats”，其中对Amen Break进行了编辑和处理，使其“成为曲目的核心，而不仅仅是节奏的铺垫”。 [3]这一断点被用于当年的许多主流曲目，包括 N.W.A 的“Straight Outta Compton”和 Rob Base 和 DJ E-Z Rock 的“Keep It Going Now”。[4]它在 20 世纪 90 年代初的英国舞曲音乐中被广泛采样，特别是在鼓、贝斯和丛林音乐中。[5][3]它已被用于多种流派，包括 Oasis 等乐队的摇滚音乐、广告以及 Futurama 等电视主题。[3][6]

Amen Break 已在数千首曲目中使用，使其成为历史上采样最广泛的曲目之一。 [3]它之所以流行，是因为它易于操作，并提供了一种简单的方式来创作丛林音乐。[3]英国鼓手汤姆·斯金纳 (Tom Skinner) 引用了录音质量中吸引人的“嘎吱声”。 [3]制作人通过改变其音高或速度，或重新排序其组件来模仿鬼音或其他效果来操纵它。 [3]

“阿门，兄弟”（包括阿门休息）的版权所有者是温斯顿乐队领队理查德·刘易斯·斯宾塞。[3]他和科尔曼都没有收到休息期间的版税。[3]斯宾塞并不知道它的用途，直到 1996 年一位高管联系他索要母带，当时他正在华盛顿地铁工作。[3][7]记者西蒙·雷诺兹将这种情况比作“一个人去精子库，不知不觉地生下了数百个孩子”。 [3]斯宾塞无法采取法律行动，因为当时侵犯版权的时效为三年。[1]

斯宾塞谴责这次采样是抄袭，并表示他“感觉被敲诈和强奸”。 [2]他在 2011 年说道：“（科尔曼）的心和灵魂都投入到了鼓声中。 现在这些人复制粘贴它并赚了数百万美元。”[3] 然而，在 2015 年，他说：“这还不是发生在你身上的最糟糕的事情。 我是美国的一名黑人，事实上有人想使用我创造的东西——这真是令人受宠若惊。”[2]

科尔曼于 2006 年去世，无家可归，一贫如洗。 斯宾塞说他不太可能意识到他对音乐产生的影响。 [2] 2015 年，英国 DJ Martyn Webster 和 Steve Theobald 为 Spencer 发起的 GoFundMe 活动筹集了超过 18,000 英镑（26,000 美元）。[2]斯宾塞于 2020 年去世。[8] 2026 年，《阿门，兄弟》因其“在国家录制的声音遗产中具有文化、历史或美学重要性”而被美国国会图书馆选入国家唱片登记处保存。 [9]
